title: Architecture-specific inference profiling: Llama / Mistral / Qwen + long-context & MoE routing
content:
Status: working notes + experiment log. Purpose: capture architecture-specific perf characteristics we saw during the last quarter of model onboarding (Llama-family, Mistral-family, Qwen-family) and for MoE variants; record micro-benchmarks, hotspot attribution, and short-term mitigations. Use this as the single-source for follow-ups: kernel work, routing optimizations, and scheduling experiments.

High-level takeaways (summary):
- Llama-style models: dense attention + relatively uniform layer perf. Dominant hotspots: large GEMM kernels in MLP, KV cache memory traffic when seq_len > 4k. Good candidates for continuous batching and fused rotary/attn kernels.
- Mistral-family: fewer parameters but wider layers -> attention matmul shapes differ (wider heads). Observed better memory locality at medium seq lengths (512-2048) but frequency of small matmuls increased, causing kernel launch overhead on multi-GPU pods.
- Qwen-family: heavy use of grouped linear layers and normalization variants. LayerNorm + gating is slightly costlier; Qwen benefits significantly from fp16/quantized kernels.
- Long-context (>4k tokens): KV cache becomes primary constraint (DRAM bandwidth + PCIe traffic when spilling). For on-host private deployments we must avoid host-device round trips and keep caches sharded by host to reduce cross-device synchronization.
- MoE routing overhead: nominal compute advantage in FLOPs for sparsely routed experts is offset by routing scatter/gather and synchronization costs unless the batch contains many diverse tokens that route to many experts. The tipping point: expert count > 16 and batch diversity high -> routing overhead > compute savings.

Experiment logs and numbers (representative runs; infra: 8xA100-80GB, PyTorch 2.3 + custom kernels):
- Baseline: Llama-13B dense fp16 (seq=1024, batch=8, temp=1.0)
  - p50 latency per token: 28 ms (streaming measurement, warm), tokens/sec per GPU: ~360
  - GPU utilization: 65% (compute), memory used: 22GB, kernel hotspots: matmul(67%), softmax(12%), layernorm(8%), to/from host 3%

- Llama-13B long-context (seq=4096, batch=2):
  - p50 latency per token: 92 ms, tokens/sec per GPU: ~120
  - Where time goes: KV cache read/write: ~42% of time, matmul 40%, memory copies + kernel launches 12%
  - Notes: peak device memory 47GB -> close to capacity; observed transient OOM in mixed workloads when batching spikes.

- Mistral-7B (seq=2048, batch=16 across pipeline):
  - p50 token latency: 22 ms, throughput: ~480 tokens/sec/GPU
  - Kernel profile: matmul 54% (many small matmuls), softmax 15%, layernorm 9%, kernel launch overhead high due to many small ops across layers.
  - Mitigation: fuse small linear sequences, increase batch packing (reduce kernel launches) -> saw 18% throughput gain.

- Qwen-7B (grouped linear pattern; seq=1024, batch=8):
  - p50 token latency: 24 ms, throughput: ~420 tokens/sec/GPU
  - Observations: layernorm variant cost + grouped linear overhead. Quantized int8 kernels improved throughput by ~35% at small quality hit (noted on internal evals).

- MoE-Base, 64 experts (sparse routing), seq=512, batch=64 distributed across 4 GPUs:
  - Effective sparse FLOPs reduced by ~3.5x vs dense, but end-to-end throughput only improved 1.2x due to routing scatter/gather and imbalance across experts.
  - Routing overhead measured: 28% of CPU-side time for routing index preparation and transfer, 15% GPU time for scatter/gather kernels, 10% for sync barriers.
  - When we artificially reduced expert count to 16 or used expert affinity (route tokens to limited set of experts), throughput gain improved to ~2.0x.

Profiling methodology (commands / tools):
- Use mixed approach: nvprof/nvtx + in-process tracing + custom kernel counters. Important traces: per-kernel duration, PCIe transfer sizes, CPU-side routing time (for MoE).
- Example run for Llama profiling: python -m rwinference.bench --model llama-13b --seq 1024 --batch 8 --trace nvtx --repeat 50 --device cuda:0
- MoE routing instrument: enable ROUTE_TIMERS env var to capture gate latency per token and dump routing histograms to /tmp/moe_route.json

Hotspots and root causes (by model family):
- Llama: big dense matmuls in MLP dominate. Also rotary embedding application is a measurable cost. KV cache is a memory-bound stage when seq grows, especially if KV split across devices.
- Mistral: lots of small matmuls -> kernel launch and occupancy inefficiency. Also GEMM shapes often not power-of-two friendly -> lower TFLOPS.
- Qwen: normalization and grouped linears increase per-layer overhead. Quantization helps but requires careful calibration for accuracy.
- MoE: routing scatter/gather and load imbalance. Also frequent small expert kernels lead to context-switching overhead on GPU; PCIe/CPU overhead if routing indices prepared on host.

Short-term mitigations (practical, deployable within 1 sprint):
- Kernel fusion for common patterns (linear->relu->linear or attention projection sequences) for Mistral and Qwen to reduce launches. Prioritize layers with small matmul shapes.
- KV cache locality: pin KV shards to the same device as their serving weights; avoid round-trip to host; ensure we prefer device-resident allocation for long-context requests. Add a per-request flag to prefer "inplace-kv" placement.
- MoE: implement expert affinity caching and batched routing where possible. Maintain per-expert input buffers to amortize scatter/gather. Add a routing-cost estimator to our router to decide when to fall back to dense variant.
- Quantization knob: expose quantization presets per model family; default to int8 for Qwen-family and allow QA thresholds to gate usage.

Mid-term work (3-8 weeks):
- Implement fused rotary + attention kernel for Llama-style rotary embeddings (expected 8-12% latency reduction at seq 1024+).
- Improve auto-batching logic to detect small-matmul-heavy models (Mistral) and coalesce requests more aggressively across lanes.
- MoE routing overhaul: move routing gate computation fully on-device for GPU-first deployments and implement hierarchical routing to reduce expert scatter count. Evaluate placement strategies for experts (collocated vs sharded) with microbenchmarks.

Risks and unknowns:
- Quantization regressions: int8 reductions can cause downstream eval model-quality regressions on some Qwen checkpoints; need more eval runs across our core eval sets.
- Cross-tenant long-context patterns: multi-tenant hosts with both short and long sequences complicate KV placement; eviction policies need to be evaluated.
- MoE behavioral differences: routing anisotropy (few tokens dominate particular experts) can create hot spots; dynamic expert rebalancing might be necessary but is complex to implement reliably.

Quick action items (owner initials):
- RP: add in-process NVTX markers for gating and routing (INF-1423).
- DC: prototype fused rotary-attention kernel PR and measure on Llama-13B (PR #5123).
- AM: run quantization sweep for Qwen-7B on eval sets and report WER/ROUGE deltas.

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally a mix of raw numbers, heuristics, and experiment logs. Expect follow-up detailed microbench notebooks under the same folder (will name pattern: perf-notebook-<model>-<date>.ipynb).
- If you run reproductions, please attach profiler traces and a short one-paragraph summary to the Jira ticket linked above.

Appendix (short checklist for reproducing long-context KV experiments):
- Use device-resident KV allocation: --kv-placement device
- Warm-up with 2x tokens of target seq length before measuring to avoid first-pass kernel slowdowns.
- Record: p50/p95 token latency, GPU mem usage, PCIe bandwidth counters, per-kernel duration.

End of notes.
